Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: Fire/flames is not a plausible primary trigger for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver unless other profile elements indicate fire-related abuse or a fire context, which they do not. The rest of the trigger, threat, memory, and appraisal items point to interpersonal threat rather than burn/fire trauma, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.explanation: Survival guilt about others dying is difficult to reconcile with childhood physical abuse by a caregiver when no other items reference deaths, fatalities, or witnessing others die. It also conflicts with the rest of the profile, which centers on helplessness and failure to stop abuse rather than surviving when others did not.

vignette: Elena Moretti was nine years old the first time the quiet in the hallway shattered. She had learned to read the house by the rhythm of footsteps, the weight of a closing door, and the specific cadence of her caregiver’s breathing when he entered her room. When his hands finally came down, it was never announced. One moment she would be reading, and the next her shoulders would lock, her body bracing before her mind could catch up to what was happening. He was the person who fed her, signed her report cards, and promised to keep the dark at bay. That promise fractured completely when the violence became the way he spoke, and Elena was left holding the impossible contradiction that the person who owed her safety had become the source of it. She could not stop it. She could not intervene. The betrayal settled into her bones, and with it came the certainty that she would never forgive herself for simply lying still while it happened. Over the years, her body kept the ledger. Long after she left the house, her chest would still seize in grocery store aisles when a cart clipped hers, her pulse hammering against her ribs before she registered that it was only metal. She learned to stand near exits, to track the room, to count the seconds between footsteps. When someone turned too quickly, her breath caught in a dry throat. She stopped trying to force herself to speak of the years she spent cowering; the images were already stamped behind her eyes like slides on a reel—clear, unblinking, impossible to close. When her husband asked what was wrong, she would open her mouth, but the words dissolved. She knew exactly what had happened, yet nothing she said matched the picture in her head. Sometimes, when the memories surfaced during quiet evenings, she felt nothing at all, as if watching a film of another woman’s life. Now at seventy-three, Elena worked as a QA Engineer, poring over systems that required absolute certainty. The work suited her need for predictable outcomes, yet the job held traps she had spent decades sidestepping. She built routines that let her control her environment: she never stayed late after the evening shift, she took the service elevator to avoid being locked in a lobby with a male colleague, and she always requested written instructions rather than verbal briefings. When a deployment timeline shifted without explanation, her hands trembled and her eyes darted to the door, her body bracing for a strike that would not come. She avoided the company’s annual memorial day, canceling her attendance the year her longtime manager passed away. Standing near the wrought-iron gates of the local cemetery for her aunt’s interment left her unable to breathe, the damp stone and the gathered grief pressing against her ribs until she slipped out through the back lot. The habits she cultivated to stay safe slowly carved her away from her daily life. She stopped attending team dinners, fearing the unpredictable flow of conversation and the sudden clatter of a dropped fork. Her husband grew accustomed to her flinching when he crossed the threshold quietly, and they settled into a careful distance that felt safer than confrontation. But last month, after a routine check-up revealed rising blood pressure, her doctor asked what sustained the constant tension in her shoulders. Elena sat on the exam table, staring at the linoleum, and for the first time in decades, she admitted that the fear had outlived its purpose. She did not want to spend her remaining years waiting for a door to open, flinching at shadows, or convincing herself that silence was the only way to keep the worst from returning. She had come to the clinic hoping to learn how to let her body unclench, hoping to find a way to sit at a dinner table without counting the exits, and hoping that somewhere past the photographs in her mind, she might finally rest.
